samples.summary: Parquet import is completely unbounded — no cell or byte budget, unlike the CSV path whose budget exists to prevent an unrecoverable persist failure
samples.evidence: `importParquetFile` calls `parquetReadObjects({ file, compressors })` (reads every row group into JS objects) and hands the whole record array to `importRecordsAsSheet`, which writes one cell per field with no cap. The CSV path enforces both `MAX_IMPORT_CELLS = 40_000` and `MAX_IMPORT_BYTES = 8_000_000` (packages/sheets/src/import/csv-importer.ts:91,155) precisely because exceeding them is, per that file's own comment, "the exact unrecoverable persist-time failure this budget exists to prevent". The only gate on the new path is `uploadSizeError` (packages/frontend/src/app/documents/file-meta.ts:46), which allows any file up to 50 MB. Parquet is a compressed columnar format: a 50 MB file routinely holds millions of rows, so a normal upload will materialize tens of millions of cells — browser OOM/tab freeze, or a Yorkie document far past the ceiling that fails at persist after the worker has already created the document (packages/frontend/src/app/documents/upload-queue.ts:351-370). `importParquet` also cannot report `truncated`/`rowCount`, so nothing tells the user anything was dropped.
searchedFor: grep MAX_IMPORT_CELLS across packages/sheets/src and packages/frontend/src
grep writeWorksheetCell for any row/column dimension cap

samples.summary: Parquet nested/list/struct columns containing INT64 values will make toCell's JSON.stringify throw a TypeError, failing the whole import
samples.evidence: `importRecordsAsSheet` calls `cellFromInput(toCell(value))` (packages/sheets/src/import/record-importer.ts:63). `toCell` does `if (typeof val === 'object' && val !== null) return JSON.stringify(val);`. hyparquet returns INT64/UINT64 values as BigInt, and LIST/MAP/STRUCT columns as arrays/objects; `JSON.stringify` on any object containing a BigInt throws `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt`. That rejects the entire import with a cryptic error for a perfectly ordinary Parquet schema (e.g. `list<int64>` or a struct with an id field). Nothing in the new code narrows or sanitizes reader values before handing them to `toCell`.
searchedFor: looked for hyparquet in node_modules (not installed in the working tree)

samples.summary: INT64 Parquet values silently lose precision: BigInt -> string -> Number round-trip corrupts values above 2^53
samples.evidence: `toCell(BigInt)` falls through to `String(val)`, then `cellFromInput` -> `inferInput` -> `parseNumberLiteral` -> `Number(literal)` (packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/input.ts:122) and the cell is stored as `inferred.value.toString()` (input.ts:364). An int64 id such as 9007199254740993 is written into the sheet as 9007199254740992 — a wrong value with no error. int64 keys (snowflake ids, epoch-nanos timestamps) are commonplace in Parquet, which is the format this feature exists to import.

samples.summary: Parquet BYTE_ARRAY (binary) columns are serialized as JSON index maps, producing garbage cells and huge memory use
samples.evidence: hyparquet yields non-UTF8 BYTE_ARRAY columns as Uint8Array. `toCell` stringifies them via `JSON.stringify`, so a 1 KB blob becomes a `{"0":12,"1":250,...}` string of several kilobytes per cell — meaningless to the user and a large multiplier on the (already unbounded) document size.

samples.summary: Imported string values starting with '=' are converted into live formulas rather than text
samples.evidence: `cellFromInput` treats any input beginning with '=' as a formula (packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/input.ts:235-240) and stores `{f: ...}`. A Parquet (or JSON) string column holding e.g. "=1+1" or "=SUM(A1:A9)" is therefore not imported as data but evaluated as a formula, so the sheet shows a different value than the source file. Behaviour is relocated from the old json-importer, but the new Parquet path inherits it.

samples.summary: A structurally valid Parquet file with zero rows is rejected as an error instead of importing an empty (header-only) sheet
samples.evidence: `importRecordsAsSheet` throws `"Parquet import contains no records"` when `records.length === 0`. Zero-row Parquet files are legitimate outputs of analytics pipelines and carry a full schema, so a header-only sheet is representable; the upload item instead fails with an error message in the queue (packages/frontend/src/app/documents/upload-queue.ts error branch). Also note the schema is discarded entirely: columns are inferred from record keys, so a column absent/null in every row is silently dropped from the sheet.
searchedFor: read upload-queue.ts sheet branch error handling

samples.summary: Doc comment on ImportedSpreadsheetFile is now stale — it enumerates only XLSX/JSON as the budget-less importers
samples.evidence: Lines 17-25 say "Only the CSV path can report these — the XLSX and JSON importers read their input whole and have no budget to stop on". The new `importParquet` (line 118) is a fourth path with the same property and is not mentioned, so a reader is left believing Parquet is bounded.

verdict.reason: The absence is real. importParquetFile (parquet-importer.ts:17-26) reads every row group via parquetReadObjects with no row/limit argument and passes the full record array to importRecordsAsSheet (record-importer.ts:35-83), which writes one cell per non-empty field and only tallies cellCount — it is never compared against any bound, and writeWorksheetCell (worksheet-grid.ts:183-200) imposes no dimension cap. The CSV budgets the reviewer cites do exist (csv-importer.ts:91 MAX_IMPORT_BYTES=8_000_000, :155 MAX_IMPORT_CELLS=40_000) with the documented "unrecoverable persist-time failure" rationale, and csv-importer.ts:162-165 explicitly notes the non-CSV importers have no budget. On the frontend, .parquet routes to the sheet branch (upload-kind.ts:27) and the only pre-flight gate is uploadSizeError's 50 MB cap (file-meta.ts:34-48); no parquet-specific limit exists in sheet-import-actions.ts:118-127 or in apply-imported-content.ts. Because importParquet returns neither truncated nor rowCount, the truncation warning at upload-queue.ts:367-370 can never fire, and since getOrCreateDoc (upload-queue.ts:354) runs before applyContent (:359), a persist-time size failure leaves an already-created empty document plus an error — an inconsistent state on a normally reachable path (a compressed 50 MB parquet holding millions of rows). I searched for the budget under alternative names (MAX_IMPORT*, budget, cap, limit, truncated) across all packages/**/src/**/*.ts, in both parquet test files, and along the enqueue/import/apply chain; no counterexample exists. In-lane for correctness: unguarded resource exhaustion causing a crash/failed persist with partially created state.

verdict.reason: The finding checks out against the repository. `toCell` (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:35) unconditionally calls `JSON.stringify` on any non-Date object, which throws `TypeError: Do not know how to serialize a BigInt` when the object graph contains a BigInt. `importRecordsAsSheet` (packages/sheets/src/import/record-importer.ts:59-63) passes reader values straight into `toCell` with only a null/undefined filter and no try/catch, so a throw aborts the entire import. `importParquetFile` (packages/sheets/src/import/parquet-importer.ts:21-26) feeds hyparquet's `parquetReadObjects` output directly in with no coercion; hyparquet (v1.29.2, packages/sheets/package.json:31) returns INT64/UINT64 as BigInt and LIST/MAP/STRUCT as arrays/objects, so a `list<int64>` or struct-with-int64 column produces an object containing BigInt. The path is reachable in normal use: packages/frontend/src/app/spreadsheet/sheet-import-actions.ts:143-144 routes any `.parquet` upload through `importParquet` -> `importParquetFile` with no sanitizing layer. A grep for BigInt/bigint across packages/sheets/src returns zero matches, so no guard exists; existing tests only cover flat scalar columns. Nested values are explicitly in scope per the design docs, so this is not an unsupported input. No refutation ground (not-present / already-guarded / out-of-scope) applies.

finding.summary: INT64 Parquet values silently lose precision: BigInt -> string -> Number round-trip corrupts values above 2^53
finding.evidence: `toCell(BigInt)` falls through to `String(val)`, then `cellFromInput` -> `inferInput` -> `parseNumberLiteral` -> `Number(literal)` (packages/sheets/src/model/worksheet/input.ts:122) and the cell is stored as `inferred.value.toString()` (input.ts:364). An int64 id such as 9007199254740993 is written into the sheet as 9007199254740992 — a wrong value with no error. int64 keys (snowflake ids, epoch-nanos timestamps) are commonplace in Parquet, which is the format this feature exists to import.

verdict.reason: Verified the full chain in the repo. toCell (packages/sheets/src/store/readonly.ts:33-37) has no bigint branch: bigint is not `object`, so it hits `String(val)`. record-importer.ts:63 pipes that string into cellFromInput, which calls inferInput -> parseNumberLiteral, whose integer branch returns `Number(literal)` (input.ts:104-123); Number("9007199254740993") === 9007199254740992 and is finite, so it is accepted as a number and persisted as `inferred.value.toString()` (input.ts:361-374). Result: cell v = "9007199254740992", a silently wrong value, on the Parquet import path (parquet-importer.ts:21-26 passes raw parquetReadObjects records straight in; the integration test's int id column already traverses it). No guard exists: record-importer.ts:60 only skips null/undefined, and a repo-wide grep finds no bigint handling in packages/sheets. The repo's own convention elsewhere (packages/backend/src/yorkie/yorkie-json.ts:143-146, with test yorkie-json.spec.ts:62) preserves out-of-safe-range bigints as decimal strings, showing the safe handling is deliberately applied elsewhere but missing here. Silent corruption of imported data is in the correctness lane (data loss / wrong result in a case the feature exists to handle), and no design doc documents double truncation as accepted for Parquet. Even if hyparquet returned numbers rather than BigInt for INT64, the imported cell is still silently wrong, so the finding holds either way.
